requirements.requirement: Only root and opsadmin can schedule cron jobs on node1 (cron.allow configured correctly, opsadmin created)
requirements.summary: Baseline showed no /etc/cron.allow and no opsadmin user (cmd-c277195bef464baa). Executor created opsadmin and wrote /etc/cron.allow containing exactly 'root' and 'opsadmin' with correct ownership/perms (cmd-1a0b0e2c59f94dff), confirmed present in final state (cmd-ecdcea28119a4581).

requirements.requirement: Users other than root/opsadmin are denied cron scheduling
requirements.summary: Initial root-proxied test (crontab -u operator -) incorrectly succeeded since root bypasses cron.allow, but executor identified this flaw and re-tested with operator invoking crontab as itself, which was correctly denied with 'not allowed to use this program' (cmd-1627fdb08081438e). Denial was reconfirmed after restart (cmd-b724936a78db4ecf).

requirements.requirement: root and opsadmin retain cron scheduling ability
requirements.summary: opsadmin successfully installed/listed a crontab when invoking crontab as itself (cmd-1627fdb08081438e); root's own crontab install/list/remove succeeded (cmd-ecdcea28119a4581); both reconfirmed after restart (cmd-b724936a78db4ecf).

requirements.requirement: No lingering test crontabs left behind; crond remains healthy
requirements.summary: /var/spool/cron confirmed empty and crond active/enabled both before restart (cmd-ecdcea28119a4581) and after restart (cmd-b724936a78db4ecf).

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide restart evidence protocol executed on node1: pre-restart healthy baseline, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, recovered service/config/data state
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id bf4e9cbb... and crond health captured (cmd-8aaa47e18f3e4029), restart acknowledgement returned before disconnection (cmd-b6fdfcb3a8044884), node unreachable during transition (cmd-e79a1061090e44d7, cmd-a857694ee7ee4d07), new boot_id 944112b2... confirmed with uptime reset (cmd-a60349bee5d7400e), and post-restart recovery of crond, cron.allow, opsadmin, and functional allow/deny enforcement all verified (cmd-b724936a78db4ecf). Cross-checked against fixed global boot-identity observations which show the same bf4e9cbb...->944112b2... transition.

overall_summary: The task (restrict cron scheduling on node1 to root and opsadmin) was fully and correctly implemented: /etc/cron.allow was created with the right users and permissions, enforcement was properly verified with self-invoked commands after an initial flawed root-proxied test was caught and corrected, and the restriction was shown to survive a full node restart along with crond health, opsadmin persistence, and functional allow/deny behavior. The independent restart protocol is well evidenced with a clean pre/during/post transition and boot-id cross-check against the fixed lifecycle snapshots. The only blemish is a handful of leftover temporary test log files in /tmp that were not cleaned up.
limitations: The preparation_comparison shows no changes because after_prepare is an alias of before_prepare (prepare was disabled), so preparer-vs-executor separation relies entirely on the executor's own baseline capture rather than an independent prepare snapshot.
Leftover files /tmp/allow_test.log, /tmp/deny_test.log, /tmp/deny_test2.log, /tmp/reboot.log were not removed by the executor and remain as minor residue.

operational_hygiene.summary: The executor's initial denial test (cmd-1a0b0e2c59f94dff) was methodologically flawed (proxied through root via crontab -u operator, which bypasses cron.allow), but this was a diagnostic misstep quickly identified and corrected with a proper self-invoked test (cmd-1627fdb08081438e); no lasting harm resulted. The clear unwanted residue: temporary log files (/tmp/deny_test.log, /tmp/allow_test.log, /tmp/deny_test2.log created by cmd-1a0b0e2c59f94dff and cmd-1627fdb08081438e, and /tmp/reboot.log created by cmd-b6fdfcb3a8044884) were left in /tmp after the task, confirmed present in the after-executor temporary-files snapshot and never cleaned up. These are small, low-risk, non-sensitive leftover files but constitute unnecessary residue since the executor cleaned up crontabs meticulously but not these logs. All other state-changing commands (useradd, cron.allow write, crontab test install/removal cycles, reboot) map directly to satisfying the task or the mandatory restart protocol, and crontabs/spool were fully restored to empty in every case.
